summary.summary: South Ribble is effectively debt-free: gross debt at 31 March 2026 was just £42k of finance leases, with the £25.1m capital financing requirement met entirely from the council's own cash and no external borrowing taken in the year. Investments stood at £22.3m at year end (average daily balance £37.1m, earning £1,503k at 3.63%), including £11m of term deposits with Blackpool and Bournemouth, Christchurch & Poole councils, and financing costs are a modest 3.28% of the net revenue stream. The trend to watch is slow cash erosion: average balances fell 16.6% year-on-year and interest earned dropped 33% as capital spending is funded internally, while the CFR rose from £19.7m to £25.1m. All prudential indicators and counterparty limits were complied with.

news_drafts.headline: South Ribble commits £20,000 borrowing for affordable housing acquisition
news_drafts.lead: South Ribble Council has approved a capital budget to acquire a three or four-bedroom family home using Section 106 contributions — money from developers building new homes locally. The council will use £250,000 from the Section 106 agreement and borrow £20,000 to meet the £270,000 purchase price, creating an annual debt service cost of roughly £2,000. The property will generate £10,200 per year in rental income, which the council's chief finance officer confirms should cover both the borrowing costs and day-to-day running expenses such as repairs and maintenance, making the investment self-financing. Officers have flagged that the Section 106 agreement includes time limits for spending the contributions and circumstances where unspent money becomes repayable, creating a compliance risk the council has decided to accept.
news_drafts.paper_title: Establishment of a Capital Budget for the Acquisition of a Three or Four-Bedroom Family Home Using Section 106 Affordable Housing Contributions

news_drafts.headline: South Ribble draws down £1.6m in reserves while leaving £1.3m budget gap unresolved for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead: South Ribble Council is drawing down its reserves, money set aside for emergencies, to balance its budget this year while still leaving a £1.3 million gap unfunded for 2027/28. The council's total reserves are forecast to fall from £21.2 million to £19.7 million by the end of March 2027. The largest depletion is a £3.3 million drawdown from the Business Rates Equalisation Reserve, which signals that income from local business rates has fallen short of forecast. A separate reserve set aside for transformation and savings programmes is being drawn down by £640,000, suggesting those planned savings are not materializing as expected. While the council has identified £498,000 of savings towards the 2027/28 gap, it states only that "further options for savings ahead of budget setting will be developed in year", leaving the funding solution still undetermined. Using reserves to cover day-to-day spending is unsustainable; if the trend continues, the council risks exhausting its financial cushion.

findings.paper_title: Establishment of a Capital Budget for the Acquisition of a Three or Four-Bedroom Family Home Using Section 106 Affordable Housing Contributions
findings.headline: Rental income of £10,200 per annum is projected to cover borrowing costs and operational expenses, making the investment self-financing.
findings.detail: The property will generate £10,200 annual rental income. After the £2,000 annual borrowing cost, the Finance Officer states the remaining income should be sufficient to cover management, maintenance and lifecycle costs, meaning the capital investment requires no ongoing subsidy from reserves.
findings.matters: Capital investments that self-finance through revenue are lower-risk and demonstrate efficient asset deployment; this reduces reliance on the general fund.
findings.figures: £10,200 annual rental income; £2,000 annual borrowing cost
findings.quote: This should be offset by the rental income which should also be sufficient to cover associated costs such as repairs and maintenance.

findings.paper_title: Establishment of a Capital Budget for the Acquisition of a Three or Four-Bedroom Family Home Using Section 106 Affordable Housing Contributions
findings.headline: Section 106 agreement contains repayment and time-limit provisions that create compliance risk for this £250,000 deployment.
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that the relevant Section 106 agreement includes time limits for expenditure and circumstances where unspent contributions become repayable. Officers have concluded the acquisition complies with the fund's objectives, but this is an acknowledged and material compliance risk.
findings.matters: Misuse of Section 106 funding could force repayment of £250,000 or create legal liability; affects the council's ability to deploy this funding class and its overall credit standing.
findings.quote: Members should be aware that the relevant Section 106 agreement contains provisions relating to the use of the contributions, including time limits for expenditure and circumstances in which unspent monies become repayable. As a result, there is a potential risk associated with the proposed use of the funding.

findings.paper_title: Establishment of a Capital Budget for the Acquisition of a Three or Four-Bedroom Family Home Using Section 106 Affordable Housing Contributions
findings.headline: Council commits to borrow £20,000 for property acquisition with annual debt service cost of approximately £2,000.
findings.detail: The total budget is £270,000. Section 106 contributions will fund £250,000, with the remaining £20,000 to be funded through borrowing. The Statutory Finance Officer confirms this creates an annual revenue cost of approximately £2,000.
findings.matters: New borrowing creates a debt service obligation; all new debt commitments are material to credit decisions.
findings.figures: £270,000 total; £250,000 from Section 106; £20,000 borrowed; £2,000 annual cost
findings.quote: The additional £20k will be funded through borrowing with an associate revenue cost per annum of around £2k.
